data.command: Describe Cozy Bear's targeting of diplomatic organizations

data.text:
Cozy Bear (also tracked as APT29, Nobelium, Midnight Blizzard, UNC2452, Dark Halo, The Dukes, CozyDuke, YTTRIUM and Iron Hemlock) is a Russian state-sponsored espionage group that NSA, CISA, the UK NCSC and Microsoft Threat Intelligence assess with high confidence belongs to the SVR, Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service. Its missions are long-dwell intelligence collection rather than disruption, and diplomatic organizations — embassies, consulates, ministries of foreign affairs, permanent missions to multilateral bodies, and the foreign-policy think tanks and policy staff around them — have been among its most consistent targets for more than a decade.

The target selection follows mission fit. Diplomatic networks are the collection path to foreign-policy decision-making, negotiating positions and cable traffic, and diplomatic staff work and travel across many networks, which gives the group a wide and constantly shifting set of footholds. APT29's diplomatic activity comes in waves that track Russian foreign-policy priorities: NATO and EU member states, and from 2022 onward states supporting Ukraine. Publicly reported activity includes the 2015-2016 compromise of political and diplomatic organizations (including the DNC, alongside APT28), enumeration of US State Department and think tank mailboxes, the 2020 SolarWinds/SUNBURST supply-chain campaign that reached diplomatic and government networks through a compromised IT vendor, and the 2020 targeting of COVID-19 vaccine research, which hit diplomatic and health-sector institutions in the UK, US and Canada.

More recent diplomatic-focused activity: from 2022 onward CISA, NSA, NCSC-UK and European partners published joint advisories on APT29 spearphishing campaigns that used malicious ISO, IMG and VHD attachments with the EnvyScout HTML-smuggling dropper, often themed as embassy notifications, visa or diplomatic invitations, against government and diplomatic entities in Europe and NATO member states. In 2023, NATO members and EU diplomatic institutions — including Polish and Czech foreign ministries — were targeted, while the group pivoted hard to cloud and identity abuse: Microsoft 365 and Azure AD, OAuth application and token theft to read mail without touching endpoints, and the FoggyWeb and MagicWeb AD FS implants for persistence. In 2024 Microsoft and NCSC reported Midnight Blizzard's intrusion into Microsoft corporate email, its password-spraying campaigns, and its use of residential proxy networks (built from compromised IoT devices) to obscure C2. Diplomats were also targeted on messaging platforms such as WhatsApp and via the WinRAR zero-day CVE-2023-38831, with credential-harvesting pages imitating diplomatic and government portals.

The recurring tradecraft against diplomatic targets: spearphishing with HTML/SVG smuggling and archive, ISO, LNK or VHD attachments; credential harvesting and phishing proxy pages; password spraying and brute forcing of VPN, OWA and cloud mail; exploitation of edge and collaboration services (Outlook CVE-2023-23397, TeamCity, Zimbra, Ivanti); abuse of OAuth consent, service principals and trusted cloud infrastructure for persistence; and custom tooling such as SUNBURST, FoggyWeb, MagicWeb, GraphicalProton, and Kazuar/SmokedHam. Because much of this is identity-based rather than malware-based, defenders of diplomatic organizations typically see it as anomalous or bulk mailbox access, unfamiliar OAuth applications, and impossible-travel sign-ins rather than as an endpoint alert.

Primary references: MITRE ATT&CK G0016 (APT29); joint CISA/NSA/NCSC-UK advisories on SVR cyber operations; UK NCSC advisories on SVR actors targeting COVID-19 research and adapting to cloud; Microsoft Threat Intelligence reporting on Nobelium/Midnight Blizzard.
